about: Sourced life stories for people of the wilderness years and the judges (Korah, Nun, Caleb, Balaam, Balak, Sihon, Abimelech son of Gideon). Written from the KJV text of the passages each person's record indexes; there is no reviewed dossier for this group.

korah-exo-6-21.short: A Levite of the house of Kohath, son of Izhar, who led a rising against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness and was swallowed when the earth opened.

paragraphs.text: Korah was a Levite, the son of Izhar, the son of Kohath. Izhar was a brother of Amram, the father of Aaron and Moses. Exodus names Korah's sons as Assir, Elkanah and Abiasaph, "the families of the Korhites".

With Dathan, Abiram and On of the tribe of Reuben, and two hundred and fifty princes of the assembly, Korah rose up before Moses, and they gathered together against Moses and Aaron. They said, "Ye take too much upon you, seeing all the congregation are holy". Moses fell on his face, then told Korah and his company to bring censers with fire and incense before the LORD the next day, and the LORD would show whom he had chosen. He reminded them that God had already brought the Levites near to serve the tabernacle, and asked, "seek ye the priesthood also?"

The next day Korah gathered all the congregation against Moses and Aaron at the door of the tabernacle, and the glory of the LORD appeared. The people were told to get away from the tents of Korah, Dathan and Abiram. The ground split, and the earth swallowed them with their houses, "all the men that appertained unto Korah", and their goods. Fire from the LORD then consumed the two hundred and fifty men who offered incense.

Their censers were made into broad plates to cover the altar, a memorial that no one not of Aaron's seed should come near to offer incense, "that he be not as Korah, and as his company". The next day the people murmured, and a plague killed fourteen thousand seven hundred, "beside them that died about the matter of Korah". Numbers later adds, "Notwithstanding the children of Korah died not." The daughters of Zelophehad would say that their father had not been "in the company of Korah".

Chronicles traces the singer Heman back through Ebiasaph to "Korah, the son of Izhar". It names Shallum, a descendant of Korah, and his brethren the Korahites as keepers of the gates of the tabernacle. It also calls five of the men who came to David at Ziklag "the Korhites", lists Korhites among the porters, and says the Korhites stood up to praise the LORD "with a loud voice on high".

Eleven psalms (42, 44 to 49, 84, 85, 87 and 88) have titles saying they are for the sons of Korah; the titles say no more about them. In the New Testament Jude says of certain men that they "perished in the gainsaying of Core".

nun-exo-33-11.short: An Ephraimite known almost only as the father of Joshua; Scripture tells nothing else of his life.

paragraphs.text: Nun appears almost only in the phrase "Joshua the son of Nun", which runs through Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua and Judges and comes again in Kings. Scripture records no word or deed of his own, and names no wife for him and no death. What it tells of him is his son.

He was of the tribe of Ephraim: the list of spies names "Oshea the son of Nun" for Ephraim, and Moses called this son Jehoshua. Chronicles traces Ephraim's line down to "Elishama his son, Non his son, Jehoshua his son", spelling the name Non. Nehemiah writes "Jeshua the son of Nun".

caleb-num-13-6.short: Caleb son of Jephunneh of Judah, one of the twelve spies, who with Joshua urged Israel to go up, and at eighty-five asked for Hebron.

paragraphs.text: Caleb was the son of Jephunneh, sent from the tribe of Judah as one of twelve men, one from each tribe, to search out Canaan. Numbers and Joshua also call him "the Kenezite". The spies came to Hebron, where the children of Anak were, and brought back a cluster of grapes from the brook Eshcol.

When the spies reported that the people of the land were strong and the cities walled, "Caleb stilled the people before Moses" and said, "Let us go up at once, and possess it". When the congregation wept and spoke of going back to Egypt, he and Joshua tore their clothes and told them not to fear, and the congregation bade stone them. The other spies died by the plague, but Joshua and Caleb "lived still".

The LORD said, "my servant Caleb, because he had another spirit with him, and hath followed me fully", would be brought into the land he had gone into. Of all the men counted in the wilderness of Sinai, none were left at the later count but Caleb and Joshua. Caleb was also named as Judah's prince for dividing the land.

At Gilgal Caleb reminded Joshua of that promise. He said he had been forty when Moses sent him and was now "fourscore and five years old", as strong as then, and asked for "this mountain", where the Anakims were. Joshua blessed him and gave him Hebron, and Caleb drove out the three sons of Anak, Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai. Joshua later records that the city of Hebron went to the priests, the children of Aaron, while its fields and villages went to Caleb.

Caleb promised his daughter Achsah to the man who took Kirjath-sepher. Othniel the son of Kenaz took it and married her; Joshua calls Othniel Caleb's brother, and Judges his younger brother. Achsah asked her father for springs of water, and he gave her "the upper springs, and the nether springs". Chronicles names Caleb's sons as Iru, Elah and Naam.

Scripture does not tell of Caleb's death. Later, 1 Samuel says Nabal of Maon "was of the house of Caleb", and an Egyptian servant of an Amalekite tells David that their raid struck "the south of Caleb". Neither verse names that Caleb's father.

balaam-num-22-5.short: Balaam son of Beor of Pethor, sent for by Balak of Moab to curse Israel, who blessed them instead and was later slain among the Midianites.

paragraphs.text: Balaam was the son of Beor and lived at Pethor, by the river; Deuteronomy calls it Pethor of Mesopotamia. Balak king of Moab sent elders of Moab and Midian to him "with the rewards of divination in their hand", asking him to curse Israel. God told him, "thou shalt not curse the people: for they are blessed", and Balaam sent them home. When Balak sent more honourable princes, Balaam said that even for "his house full of silver and gold" he could not go beyond the word of the LORD, and that night God told him that if the men came to call him he should go with them, but do only the word God would say to him.

Balaam saddled his ass and went, and God's anger was kindled because he went. The angel of the LORD stood in the way with a drawn sword; the ass saw him and turned aside three times, and Balaam struck her. Then the LORD opened the ass's mouth, and she asked, "What have I done unto thee, that thou hast smitten me these three times?" When his own eyes were opened Balaam fell on his face and said, "I have sinned", and the angel let him go on, to speak only the word he was given.

Balak took him to the high places of Baal, then to the top of Pisgah, then to the top of Peor, and seven altars were built each time. Each time Balaam "took up his parable" and blessed Israel: the first asks, "How shall I curse, whom God hath not cursed?", the second says, "God is not a man, that he should lie", and the third, "How goodly are thy tents, O Jacob". Balak smote his hands together in anger and told him to flee to his place.

Before going, Balaam spoke a fourth parable, which says, "there shall come a Star out of Jacob, and a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel", followed by shorter sayings on Amalek, on the Kenites, and of ships from Chittim. Then he "rose up, and went and returned to his place".

Numbers later says that the women of Midian caused Israel to sin in the matter of Peor "through the counsel of Balaam". When Israel made war on Midian, they slew Balaam the son of Beor with the sword along with five kings of Midian; Joshua calls him "the soothsayer". Deuteronomy says the LORD would not hearken unto Balaam but turned the curse into a blessing, and Nehemiah says the same of the curse; in Joshua 24 the LORD says, "I would not hearken unto Balaam; therefore he blessed you still". Micah bids Israel remember what Balaam answered Balak.

The New Testament names him three times. Second Peter says some have gone astray, "following the way of Balaam the son of Bosor, who loved the wages of unrighteousness", and that "the dumb ass speaking with man's voice forbad the madness of the prophet". Jude speaks of those who "ran greedily after the error of Balaam for reward", and Revelation says Balaam "taught Balac to cast a stumblingblock before the children of Israel".

balak-num-22-2.short: Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab, who sent for Balaam to curse Israel in the plains of Moab and heard him bless them instead.

paragraphs.text: Balak was the son of Zippor and king of the Moabites when Israel camped in the plains of Moab. He saw what Israel had done to the Amorites, and Moab was "sore afraid of the people, because they were many". Moab told the elders of Midian that this company would lick up all around them, "as the ox licketh up the grass of the field".

Balak sent messengers to Balaam son of Beor: "Come now therefore, I pray thee, curse me this people; for they are too mighty for me". When Balaam refused, Balak sent more honourable princes and promised to promote him to very great honour. When Balaam came, Balak met him at a city on the border of Arnon and asked why he had not come sooner.

Balak offered oxen and sheep, then took Balaam to the high places of Baal, to the top of Pisgah and to the top of Peor, with seven altars and a bullock and a ram on every altar each time. Each time Balaam blessed Israel. Balak said, "I took thee to curse mine enemies, and, behold, thou hast blessed them altogether", and then, "Neither curse them at all, nor bless them at all."

After the third blessing Balak's anger was kindled; he smote his hands together and told Balaam to flee to his place, saying the LORD had kept him back from honour. Balaam spoke again, and one of his sayings tells of a Sceptre out of Israel that "shall smite the corners of Moab". Then Balaam went home, "and Balak also went his way".

Later Scripture remembers him. Joshua 24 says that Balak "arose and warred against Israel" and called Balaam to curse them; Jephthah asks whether Balak ever strove against Israel or fought against them; Micah tells Israel to remember "what Balak king of Moab consulted". Revelation says Balaam "taught Balac to cast a stumblingblock before the children of Israel".

sihon-num-21-21.short: Sihon king of the Amorites at Heshbon, who refused Israel passage, fought them at Jahaz, and lost his land from Arnon to Jabbok.

paragraphs.text: Sihon was king of the Amorites and lived at Heshbon. He had fought the former king of Moab and taken all his land as far as the Arnon. A saying quoted in Numbers speaks of "a flame from the city of Sihon" that consumed Ar of Moab.

Israel sent messengers asking to pass through his land by the king's high way, without turning into fields or vineyards; Deuteronomy adds an offer to pay for food and water. Sihon would not let them pass, and he gathered all his people and fought Israel at Jahaz. Deuteronomy says the LORD "hardened his spirit, and made his heart obstinate", to deliver him into Israel's hand.

Israel smote him and took his land from Arnon to Jabbok, and dwelt in Heshbon and its villages; Deuteronomy says they smote him, his sons and all his people, and took all his cities and utterly destroyed their people. Moses gave the kingdom of Sihon, with that of Og king of Bashan, to Gad, Reuben and half the tribe of Manasseh. Joshua sets out the bounds of his kingdom and names five princes of Midian, smitten with him, as "dukes of Sihon".

His defeat is recalled again and again, usually with Og king of Bashan: in Moses' speeches, in Joshua, Judges and Nehemiah, and in Psalms 135 and 136. Jeremiah's prophecy against Moab uses the words "a flame from the midst of Sihon".

abimelech-jdg-8-31.short: Gideon's son by a concubine in Shechem, who killed his brothers, reigned three years, and died at Thebez when a woman dropped a millstone on him.

paragraphs.text: Gideon, also called Jerubbaal, had seventy sons, for he had many wives, and his concubine in Shechem bore him a son, Abimelech. After Gideon died, Abimelech went to his mother's brothers in Shechem. He asked them to put it to the men of Shechem whether it was better that seventy sons of Jerubbaal reign over them, or one, adding, "remember also that I am your bone and your flesh".

The men of Shechem gave him seventy pieces of silver from the house of Baal-berith, and he hired "vain and light persons". He went to his father's house at Ophrah and slew his brothers, seventy persons, "upon one stone"; only Jotham, the youngest, was left, because he hid himself. The men of Shechem and the house of Millo made Abimelech king by the plain of the pillar in Shechem.

From the top of mount Gerizim Jotham told a parable. The olive, the fig and the vine would not leave their fatness, sweetness and wine to be promoted over the trees, but the bramble said, "come and put your trust in my shadow", or else let fire come out and devour the cedars. If Shechem had dealt truly with Jerubbaal's house, Jotham said, let them rejoice in Abimelech; if not, let fire come from each to devour the other. Then he fled to Beer for fear of his brother.

Abimelech "reigned three years over Israel". Then God sent an evil spirit between him and the men of Shechem, and they dealt treacherously with him, so that the blood of the seventy would be laid on him and on them. The men of Shechem put their confidence in Gaal son of Ebed; Zebul, the ruler of the city, sent word, and Abimelech defeated Gaal, whom Zebul then thrust out of the city. Abimelech then took Shechem, slew its people, beat down the city and sowed it with salt, and set fire to the hold of the god Berith over the men of the tower of Shechem, about a thousand men and women.

At Thebez he took the city and went to burn its strong tower, but "a certain woman cast a piece of a millstone upon Abimelech's head". So that men would not say a woman slew him, he had his armourbearer thrust him through, and he died. Judges says, "Thus God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech, which he did unto his father, in slaying his seventy brethren", and that the curse of Jotham came upon the men of Shechem. After him Tola arose to defend Israel. In 2 Samuel, Joab tells a messenger that David may ask, "Who smote Abimelech the son of Jerubbesheth?"
